item.title: PostgreSQL UPSERT Strategies Avoiding Side Effects with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
item.description:
“PostgreSQL UPSERT Strategies Avoiding Side Effects with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING”

When implementing an UPSERT operation in PostgreSQL, utilizing ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE offers a straightforward approach. However, this strategy introduces potential negative side effects, especially when dealing with identical incoming rows where no data actually changes. These undesirable consequences include:

  1. Trigger Activation: Unnecessary execution of triggers defined on the table.
  2. Write-Locking: Incurring write-locks on “innocent” rows, impacting concurrent transactions.
  3. MVCC Overhead: For every target row, PostgreSQL writes a new row version, regardless of whether the data modified. This contributes significantly to table bloat, index bloat, and increased VACUUM costs, becoming a substantial performance issue with frequent duplicates.

Furthermore, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE requires specifying a conflict_target, which becomes impractical or impossible when multiple unique indexes or constraints exist that might trigger the conflict.

item.description:

This setting defines an ordered list of schemas that PostgreSQL consults to find objects like tables when they are referenced without a schema qualifier. The first schema in the path where the object is found is the one used.

The schema listed first in the search_path is considered the “current schema” or “default schema.” This is significant because any CREATE TABLE statements that omit a schema name will result in the table being created within this current schema.

item.title: PostgreSQL Timestamps: Time Zones Explained
item.description:
“PostgreSQL Timestamps: Time Zones Explained”

PostgreSQL offers two distinct timestamp data types: timestamp with time zone (often abbreviated as timestamptz) and timestamp without time zone (abbreviated as timestamp). timestamptz is generally considered the preferred choice for managing date and time information due to its robust time zone handling capabilities.

Internal Storage and Epoch:

Internally, both timestamp types use 8 bytes for storage, representing microseconds from the PostgreSQL epoch, which is January 1, 2000, 00:00:00 UTC. PostgreSQL also natively understands Unix time, which counts seconds from the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC). This is utilized in functions like to_timestamp(double precision) and EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM timestamptz).
